This Champions League opener might be the toughest possible night for Real Madrid to be missing three midfielders at once.

[Editor note: cut to a quick montage of Real Madrid's suspended trio, Champions League anthem playing, fans reacting online to the lineup dilemma, headlines calling it Mourinho's biggest early test, before cutting back to me]

Let's start with the fixture itself, because this season's league phase opens with some genuinely spicy matchups.

The best club football tournament in the world is back, the twenty twenty-six to twenty-seven UEFA Champions League campaign, and the opening matchday alone is stacked. Porto host Manchester City. Club Brugge face Aston Villa. Barcelona travel to face Feyenoord. Lille meet Real Betis in what should be a genuinely interesting one too. But the match getting our full attention today is Real Madrid hosting Inter Milan at the Santiago Bernabéu.

Let's talk about the problem hanging over this exact match, because it's a genuinely brutal one for Real Madrid to walk into.

Three midfielders are missing for this specific fixture, Bernardo Silva, Arda Güler, and Eduardo Camavinga, all through suspension rather than injury. Here's the actual breakdown, and it's worth getting right. Güler and Camavinga were both sent off in the same match last season, the Champions League quarterfinal second leg against Bayern Munich, the four-three defeat that ended Real Madrid's European campaign at that stage. Camavinga picked up his second yellow late in the match. Güler's came after the final whistle, for arguing with the referee. Bernardo Silva's suspension is a completely separate story, and it's genuinely ironic. He was sent off in the round of sixteen second leg last season, for deliberately handling the ball to stop a goal, gifting Vinicius Junior the resulting penalty. The twist is that Silva was playing for Manchester City in that match, against Real Madrid. He's since joined Real Madrid on a free transfer this summer, meaning he's now serving a ban he picked up playing against his own new club.

Let's talk about why the timing of this specific match makes the absence sting even more.

Real Madrid fans might reasonably be wondering why this fixture had to land now, rather than a match or two later. Their next Champions League match after this one is away at Roma, followed by a trip to face Arsenal, a genuinely tricky stretch. Overall, Madrid's league phase draw looks relatively kind, but these two away fixtures specifically, Roma and this Inter match, are the ones with real teeth.

Let's talk about the lineup question, because with three regular midfield options gone at once, this genuinely opens things up.

If all three were available, the answer would be simple, no changes at all, Fede Valverde and Bernardo Silva in the double pivot, the exact pairing Real Madrid have leaned on for most of this league season already. Camavinga's own recent partnership with Valverde hadn't been working particularly well either, not enough mobility, not enough dynamism, nobody willing to take players on or carry real vertical threat. Bernardo brings something different there, genuine understanding of space and timing, even without being a natural defensive midfielder in the traditional sense.

With him unavailable too, reports point toward either Dani Ceballos or Sergio Martinez as the likely deputy option. Ceballos has more experience in this exact competition already, five appearances, some real Champions League minutes under his belt, which gives him a slight edge over Martinez, who's still fairly new to the club.

Let's talk about the more interesting tactical option on the table, because it changes the whole shape of the team.

One genuine possibility being discussed involves playing Jude Bellingham and Valverde together in the double pivot, with Brahim Diaz used as the number ten and Yan Diomandé out wide. That setup keeps two properly robust midfielders anchoring the base while giving Brahim license to operate in his more natural attacking role. The catch is that this is exactly the kind of deployment Mourinho has said he doesn't want for Bellingham long-term. But for one single match, given the circumstances, it genuinely makes sense. Mourinho himself has made his priorities clear in the pre-match press conference too, saying plainly that he doesn't just want to play well, he wants to win, pointing to last season's defeat to Real Betis as an example of a match where Madrid played well but still lost. Given that mentality, and given that nobody plays a natural double pivot role better right now than Bellingham does, starting Brahim and pushing Diomandé wide feels like a genuinely strong option.

Let's talk about the other, riskier idea floating around, because it's worth mentioning even if it's unlikely.

There's also talk of Trent Alexander-Arnold potentially playing in central midfield rather than at right-back, which would let Bellingham stay further forward and push Dani Carvajal or another option into the back line. Trent has played centrally before, mostly in preseason, but never in a match of this magnitude. It's a real risk. It could also work. Given how much Trent can open up passing lanes and pick out early crosses from deep, there's a genuine case for using him in this specific match regardless of exact position, right-back or midfield.

Let's talk about the option nobody should actually want to see, because it's the shakiest of them all.

One more idea circulating involves playing Dean Huijsen in the pivot alongside Valverde, essentially using a converted center-back in midfield while bringing in an extra defender elsewhere. Huijsen is a genuinely good passer, but that position demands far more than passing range, and he's never actually played there in a real match. Asking a converted center-back to learn an entirely new defensive midfield role for the first time against a team like Inter feels like a genuinely unnecessary gamble.

Let's talk about Inter Milan's likely setup now, because understanding their identity matters just as much as Madrid's own selection headache.

Reports differ slightly on whether Marcus Thuram's partner up top will be Pio Esposito or Ange-Yoan Bonny, though either option works fine given both bring real physical presence and defensive solidity. In goal, it's Josep Martinez against Thibaut Courtois, a genuine battle of elite goalkeepers on both sides. At the back, expect Manuel Akanji alongside Alessandro Bastoni, with the back three completed by a third center-back. In midfield, the earlier reporting pointed toward Hakan Calhanoglu, Nicolo Barella, and Petar Sucic starting, though there's been some late speculation about Kristjan Asllani potentially getting the nod in Sucic's place instead. Given Sucic already has real Champions League pedigree from his time at Liverpool, and given how well that midfield trio is currently functioning, starting him again feels like the safer, more sensible call, even if Asllani gets second-half minutes.

Let's talk about how Inter actually plays, because there's a genuine misconception worth clearing up here.

Plenty of people assume Inter is a high-pressing team. That's simply not accurate. Inter defends primarily in a mid-block or low block, allowing opposition possession before committing to a tackle, rather than pressing aggressively high up the pitch. This season in Serie A, they've actually ranked ninth in the league for winning the ball back in the final third, well behind possession-obsessed teams like Napoli or high-pressing sides like Milan and Roma. That could change in the Champions League specifically, but based on domestic form so far, Inter genuinely prefers sitting in and inviting you onto them rather than hunting the ball high up the pitch.

Let's talk about what Inter actually does well instead, because the statistics paint a pretty clear picture.

They rank highest in Serie A for average positions held on the pitch, meaning they dominate territorially and keep the ball through patient, connected short passing, building through genuine numerical superiority across the back three, which can expand into a back five depending on the phase of play. At the same time, they also rank highest in the league for accurate long balls per match, and highest for accurate crosses per game too, roughly nine per match. That combination, patient buildup mixed with the ability to suddenly go long or wide through their attacking wing-backs, makes them genuinely difficult to pin down tactically. They've also scored more set-piece goals than any other side in the league so far this season, three from dead-ball situations alone.

Let's talk about the one real defensive weakness Inter have actually shown, because it's directly relevant to how Real Madrid could hurt them.

Across their matches so far this season, Inter have conceded three goals, and in their toughest recent test, against Napoli, they actually went two goals down before mounting a real comeback, driven largely by Lautaro Martinez's sheer will to fight back into the match. But in that same game, Napoli were genuinely able to carve out real chances on the counter, exposing gaps in Inter's defensive transition specifically. And Real Madrid, with Vinicius, Kylian Mbappe, Jude Bellingham, Diomandé, and Brahim Diaz all available in attack, is fundamentally a counter-attacking team built precisely to exploit exactly that kind of moment.

Let's talk about the specific risk sitting inside Inter's defensive shape, because it's worth understanding in real detail.

When Inter loses possession, their double pivot needs to drop back into position extremely quickly. In recent matches, their actual back line has generally recovered its shape in time, but the midfield line hasn't always dropped back quickly enough, opening up dangerous pockets of space in what's commonly called zone fourteen and zone fifteen, right in front of the opposition box. Against a team like Inter, leaving those pockets open even briefly is a genuinely costly mistake. That's precisely why Real Madrid's own recovery runs, from their wide players especially, matter so much in this specific match, and it's exactly why playing Brahim Diaz alongside Trent makes real defensive sense too, giving Madrid better structural balance when they lose the ball themselves.

Let's talk about Real Madrid's own defensive risk in return, because Inter genuinely knows how to exploit exactly this kind of situation.

When Real Madrid defends in transition, their own double pivot needs to fall back into position with real urgency. In recent matches, that hasn't always happened cleanly, and against a team like Inter, which loves creating overloads through their attacking wing-backs bursting forward alongside two strikers, that kind of hesitation gets punished fast. Picture Inter's front players stretching Real Madrid's back line into a genuine one-versus-one situation on the wings, with wing-backs like Federico Dimarco or Carlos Augusto whipping in crosses toward a box already crowded with runners. That's the exact kind of moment where Real Madrid could genuinely get hurt if their pivot's recovery timing isn't sharp.

Let's talk about the actual context of the match, because both teams genuinely need something from this result.

This isn't purely a must-win game for Real Madrid alone. Inter needs points here just as badly. There's real history attached to this fixture too, given Jose Mourinho's own connection to Inter, where he won a treble including the Champions League. That storyline alone adds extra weight to this particular meeting.

So how does this actually play out? Given how thin Real Madrid's midfield options are right now, and given how well-structured and patient Inter's approach tends to be, this genuinely has the makings of a tight, cagey affair, something closer to a one-one or two-two draw feels like a reasonable expectation right now, though the sample size for properly judging either side this season is still fairly small. Whoever actually takes their chances when they arrive is likely to walk away with all three points. Real Madrid have more than enough individual quality to hurt Inter on the counter. Inter have more than enough patience and structure to make Madrid's night genuinely difficult. It should be a properly fascinating one to watch.
